chapters.name: Impulse Buying
chapters.angle: You came in for one thing, but a sale makes an unplanned purchase feel like saving money.
facts: A discount still costs money if you would not otherwise buy the item.
Small unplanned purchases add up across a month.
Limited-time offers can pressure you to buy before comparing options.
Waiting before purchasing gives the initial excitement time to fade.
chapters.icon: a shopping bag with a lightning bolt
chapters.outfit: an orange hoodie and white sneakers

chapters.name: Credit Card Minimums
chapters.angle: The minimum payment keeps you from missing a payment, but it is not a plan for getting out of debt quickly.
facts: The minimum payment is usually only a small portion of the balance.
Unpaid balances generally accrue interest unless a special interest-free offer applies.
Without new charges, paying more than the minimum usually clears interest-bearing debt faster.
Taking longer to repay an interest-bearing balance generally increases total interest paid.
chapters.icon: a credit card beside one tiny coin
chapters.outfit: a red polo shirt and dark trousers

chapters.name: Unused Subscriptions
chapters.angle: You stopped using the service, but the service never stopped charging you.
facts: Subscriptions can renew automatically until canceled.
Deleting an app usually does not cancel its subscription.
Annual renewals are easier to overlook because they happen infrequently.
Several small recurring charges can become a substantial ongoing expense.
chapters.icon: a dusty television with a price tag

chapters.name: Late Payments
chapters.angle: Forgetting a deadline can make the exact same purchase more expensive without giving you anything extra.
facts: Many lenders and service providers charge late-payment fees.
Automatic payments can fail when the linked account lacks sufficient funds.
Credit payments that become sufficiently overdue can damage your credit history.
Payment reminders help you check that a bill was actually paid.
chapters.outfit: a rumpled white shirt and loose blue tie

chapters.name: Brand Loyalty
chapters.angle: A familiar logo can feel like proof of quality, even when you have not compared what you are getting.
facts: A brand name alone does not establish durability or performance.
Some store-brand products offer similar ingredients or specifications for less.
Products with similar features can sell at different prices.
Automatically choosing one brand means skipping comparison with alternatives.
chapters.icon: a price tag wearing a crown
chapters.outfit: a black hoodie with an oversized gold logo

chapters.name: Buying Too Cheap
chapters.angle: The cheapest option today can become the most expensive option per year if you keep replacing it.
facts: Repeated replacements add new purchase costs.
Repairs, energy use, and consumables contribute to total ownership cost.
A product's useful lifespan affects its cost per use.
A higher price alone does not guarantee better quality or longer life.
chapters.icon: a shoe with a detached sole
chapters.outfit: a faded blue T-shirt and patched jeans

chapters.name: Skipping Maintenance
chapters.angle: Putting off a small fix feels cheaper until the neglected problem damages something much more expensive.
facts: Routine care can prevent wear from developing into larger failures.
An ignored water leak can damage surrounding materials.
Underinflated tires can increase fuel use and tire wear.
Manufacturer schedules identify recommended maintenance tasks and intervals.
chapters.icon: a bicycle wheel with a rusty chain
chapters.outfit: green mechanic overalls and work boots

chapters.name: Chasing Rewards
chapters.angle: A reward is not a win if earning it makes you spend money you would otherwise have kept.
facts: Cashback returns only a fraction of the purchase price.
Spending thresholds can encourage purchases you did not originally plan.
Credit card interest and fees can exceed the value of rewards.
Points may have expiration dates or redemption restrictions.
chapters.icon: a rewards card with a gold star
chapters.outfit: a hot-pink varsity jacket with star patches

chapters.name: Ignoring Employer Match
chapters.angle: Some jobs offer extra retirement money when you contribute, but you have to participate to receive it.
facts: Some employers match employee contributions to a retirement plan.
Contributing below the matching threshold can leave part of the available match unused.
Employer contributions may have vesting rules that affect what you keep if you leave.
Retirement accounts can have taxes or restrictions on early withdrawals.
chapters.icon: two coins joined by a plus sign
chapters.outfit: a navy work uniform with a name badge

chapters.name: No Emergency Fund
chapters.angle: An unexpected bill can become a debt problem when there is no cash buffer between you and borrowing.
facts: Necessary repairs and other unexpected expenses do not always arrive on payday.
Without accessible savings, an unexpected expense may require borrowing.
Interest-bearing borrowing adds financing costs to the original expense.
Keeping emergency savings separate can make them less tempting to spend.
chapters.outfit: a yellow raincoat and rubber boots

chapters.name: Waiting to Invest
chapters.angle: Once bills and emergency savings are covered, waiting to feel rich can cost long-term money years of potential growth.
facts: Reinvested returns can generate further returns.
Starting later leaves less time for potential compounding.
Investment growth is not guaranteed, and investments can lose value.
Money needed soon should not depend on uncertain market gains.
chapters.icon: an hourglass beside a small sprout
chapters.outfit: a mint-green sweatshirt with a seedling emblem

chapters.name: Lifestyle Creep
chapters.angle: Your pay rises, but every extra dollar gets assigned to a nicer car, a bigger place, or a pricier routine.
facts: Lifestyle creep happens when spending rises alongside income.
Higher recurring expenses continue after the excitement of an upgrade fades.
A raise increases savings only if some of the additional income remains unspent.
Leases, loans, and contracts can make expensive upgrades costly to reverse.
chapters.icon: a shopping cart with an upward arrow
chapters.outfit: a flashy turquoise tracksuit and gold-colored watch
